evidence.title: External Validation and Comparison of a General Ward Deterioration Index Between Diversely Different Health Systems
evidence.outcome: Comparison of development vs local populations, data and missingness, and effect on model performance
evidence.effect: Hospitals differed in missingness (>5% difference in 9/52 features), deterioration rate (4.5% vs 2.5%), and racial makeup (20% vs 49% non-White); performance remained consistent.
evidence.quote: The hospitals were found to have significant differences in missingness rates (> 5% difference in 9/52 features), deterioration rate (4.5% vs 2.5%), and racial makeup (20% non-White vs 49% non-White).

evidence.title: Psychosis metabolic risk calculator (PsyMetRiC) in early psychosis: External validation study in Finland
evidence.outcome: development-validation population comparison
evidence.effect: Finnish and UK samples differed; White European/NR 100% vs 55.3%, male 58.60% vs 67.59%.
evidence.quote: The Finnish sample differed from the UK PsyMetRiC development sample on most sociodemographic, lifestyle and biochemical characteristics (Table 1 ).

evidence.title: Ensemble uncertainty estimation improves skin cancer malignancy prediction
evidence.outcome: training-distribution representativeness assessment
evidence.effect: SAGE quantified likeness of images from Argentina, Brazil and the United States to HAM10000 and identified problematic artifacts affecting reliability.
evidence.quote: Using our method, Supervised Autoencoders for Generalization Estimates (SAGE), we quantify likeness of images from patients in Argentina, Brazil and the United States to the popular HAM10000 benchmarking dataset and identify problematic image artifacts that affect the reliability of predictions in a pre-clinical setting.
evidence.country: Multinational (four public datasets across five countries, including Argentina, Brazil, United States)

evidence.title: ImmunoResponse Predictor: a GUI for accurate response prediction to immunotherapy
evidence.outcome: Whether cohort-level applicability metric detects dataset shift relative to training data and tracks accuracy
evidence.effect: Applicability 74%, 76%, 71% with accuracy 69%, 83%, 86%; UNC-108 applicability 48% with accuracy 53%, flagged as shifted. Cosine distance alone was inconsistent (73% for UNC-108).
evidence.quote: In contrast, the UNC-108 cohort exhibited applicability below 60% and achieved a prediction accuracy of only 53%, indicating a substantial shift relative to the training data.
evidence.sample_unit: patients across four external test cohorts (PCD mUC 94, PCD mRCC 58, Moreno 11, UNC-108 89)

evidence.title: Evaluating real-world deployment of an HL7-CDA-aligned LLM for ICD-10-CM coding
evidence.outcome: Cross-institutional coding performance under documentation and population distribution differences
evidence.effect: From KMUH RCT to TMMH, BioMistral full-code F-score declined from 0.754 to 0.620; BERT precision declined from 0.875 to 0.137. External evaluation used no additional retraining.
evidence.quote: Performance declined for all models on the TMMH dataset, reflecting the expected impact of institution-specific documentation variability, including differences in documentation conventions and section availability.
evidence.sample_unit: discharge summaries coded in RCT (10 certified coding specialists)

evidence.title: Remote Monitoring in Dementia Care - Lightweight, Explainable AI Validated for Early Warning of Health Events in the Home
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and generalizability on internal 65-patient cohort versus later larger 90-patient cohort
evidence.effect: 65-patient cohort: 84.64±2.36% sensitivity, 92.16±2.33% generalizability at 7% max alert rate; 90-patient cohort: 77.04±1.35% sensitivity, 90.67±1.51% generalizability.
evidence.quote: In a larger 90-patient cohort (40,586 person-days; May 2022–Feb 2024), it achieved 77.04±1.35% sensitivity and 90.67±1.51% generalizability, a strong result given the inherent noise and variability of home sensor data.

evidence.title: Prediction of cardiovascular risk factors from retinal fundus photographs: Validation of a deep learning algorithm in a prospective non-interventional study in Kenya
evidence.outcome: Differences between development (UK Biobank) and Kenyan deployment population characteristics
evidence.effect: Kenyan participants were younger, likely Black/African, with higher BMI and higher prevalence of DM and hypertension than UK Biobank development population.
evidence.quote: Compared with the UK Biobank population used for algorithm development, participants from Kenya were younger and would probably report Black/African ethnicity, with a higher body mass index and prevalence of DM and hypertension.

evidence.title: AI‑Enhanced Smartwatch AHI Estimation and AI‑Scored Polysomnography for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Real‑World Validation
evidence.outcome: Smartwatch algorithm performance in a Korean cohort versus South-American training cohorts (inter-ethnic validation)
evidence.effect: eAHI correlated strongly with aiAHI (rho 0.88, ICC 0.87); sensitivity 92.3%, specificity 92.6% for moderate-to-severe OSA; systematic underestimation, especially in mild OSA.
evidence.quote: The model was trained in South‑American cohorts, allowing inter‑ethnic validation.
evidence.sample_unit: adults with valid simultaneous smartwatch and PSG recordings

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.outcome: Mapping accuracy when generalizing to an unseen hospital
evidence.effect: BioLORD top-1 accuracy decreased from 91.6% in the fully fine-tuned setting to 73.5% when evaluated on hospitals excluded from training.
evidence.quote: Evaluating the onboarding of a new hospital (Exp1-S3) revealed a reduction in mean performance, with BioLORD's top-1 accuracy decreasing from 91.6% in the fully fine-tuned setting to 73.5%.
evidence.sample_unit: source concepts (6,179 medication names and 2,261 laboratory test names)

evidence.title: Explainable TabNet for gestational diabetes prediction with physician-in-the-loop and multi-site clinical validation
evidence.outcome: Performance drop from internal cross-validation to prospective external multi-site data
evidence.effect: Internal F1 96.22%; external multi-site F1 ranged from 83.70% to 87.00% across three hospitals, attributed partly to inter-site variability in feature availability and recording protocols.
evidence.quote: External multi-site F1 scores ranged from 83.70% to 87.00% across all three hospitals, reflecting an expected performance reduction in prospective real-world data, partly attributed to inter-site variability in feature availability and clinical data recording protocols.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (prospective external validation across three hospitals)

evidence.title: Real-World Sarilumab Use and Rule Testing to Predict Treatment Response in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: Findings from the RISE Registry
evidence.outcome: Real-world odds of LDA and MCID for rule-positive vs rule-negative sarilumab patients
evidence.effect: Rule-positive patients had higher odds of LDA (OR 1.5 [0.7, 3.2]) and MCID (1.1 [0.5, 2.4]), with wide confidence intervals including 1. Sensitivity analysis (CRP > 5 mg/l) showed better response in rule-positive patients.
evidence.quote: Among the predictive rule cohort (N = 205), rule-positive (vs. rule-negative) patients were more likely to reach LDA (odds ratio: 1.5 [0.7, 3.2]) and MCID (1.1 [0.5, 2.4]).

evidence.title: Detecting changes in the performance of a clinical machine learning tool over time
evidence.outcome: Performance under population shift from training cohort (higher positivity, COVID-19)
evidence.effect: Positivity 13.4% vs 11.5% in training, contamination 10.3% vs 6.3%, 328 COVID-19 cases; performance stayed within statistical control
evidence.quote: However, despite evolving practices and populations, the performance of our model consistently remained within the bounds of statistical control, negating the necessity for recalibration and indicating our model is robust to changing environments.

evidence.title: A geometry and dose-volume based performance monitoring of artificial intelligence models in radiotherapy treatment planning for prostate cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Differences between vendor training data and local deployment population volumes
evidence.effect: PTV 154±45 vs 120±50 cm3, bladder 141±51 vs 226±136 cm3, rectum 58±18 vs 76±29 cm3 (all p<0.001), training vs local
evidence.quote: The geometrical analysis showed significant volume differences between the training and the local dataset for respectively PTV ((154 ± 45)cm 3 ; (120 ± 50)cm 3 with p < 0.001), bladder ((141 ± 51)cm 3 ; (226 ± 136)cm 3 with p < 0.001) and rectum ((58 ± 18)cm 3 ; (76 ± 29)cm 3 with p < 0.001).

evidence.title: The incremental design of a machine learning framework for medical records processing

evidence.title: Evaluation of an AI algorithm trained on an ethnically diverse dataset to screen a previously unseen population for diabetic retinopathy
evidence.outcome: Referable DR detection accuracy in a population unseen during AI development
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 95.30% (95% CI 91.9-98.7%) and specificity 83.89% (95% CI 79.9-87.9%) for RDR; sensitivity 100% for STDR. No performance drop in the new population.
evidence.quote: On 478 subjects included in the analysis, the algorithm achieved a high classification sensitivity of 95.30% (95% CI: 91.9%-98.7%) and a specificity of 83.89% (95% CI: 79.9%-87.9%) for the detection of RDR.

evidence.title: Development, deployment, and continuous monitoring of a machine learning model to predict respiratory failure in critically ill patients
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination when applied to an external site dataset (MIMIC-IV)
evidence.effect: The UCSD-trained model's AUC dropped to 0.73 on MIMIC-IV, compared with 0.897 cross-validated and 0.908 prospective at UCSD.
evidence.quote: The final Vent.io model trained using UCSD data obtained an AUC of 0.73, lower than the minimum of 0.85 set by the PCCP, prompting a fine-tuning process.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU encounters (26,045 development, 276 prospective silent-mode, 35,534 MIMIC-IV)

evidence.title: Implementing an AI algorithm in the clinical setting: a case study for the accuracy paradox
evidence.outcome: Disease prevalence at local site versus manufacturer's validation populations
evidence.effect: Local prevalence 4.1% versus 45.0-62.2% in manufacturer's reported values; PPV 33% locally versus 95-98% reported.
evidence.quote: This disparity can be attributed to differences in disease prevalence of 4.1% at our institution compared with 45.0-62.2% from the manufacturer's reported values.
evidence.sample_unit: patients undergoing CTA in the emergency department

evidence.title: Leveraging AI to Drive Timely Improvements in Patient Experience Feedback: Algorithm Validation
evidence.outcome: Transferability to different service settings
evidence.effect: Initial theme accuracy was 57% in community/mental health, 67% in pediatrics, and 64% in GP/community, below the 75% threshold.
evidence.quote: However, the accuracy of the model was lower in organizations delivering different services, such as pediatrics and mental health.
evidence.sample_unit: NHS trusts (500-comment stratified manually coded sample per trust for accuracy)

evidence.title: Automated assessment of right ventricular systolic function from coronary angiograms with video-based artificial intelligence algorithms: development, validation, comparison against humans, and prospective deployment
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination on external site versus internal test set
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.80 (95% CI 0.76-0.84) internally versus 0.75 (95% CI 0.72-0.77) at UCSF (n=2247 studies; 30% reduced RVSF vs 10.5%); modest drop with different prevalence.
evidence.quote: External validation demonstrated AUROC 0.75 (95% CI: 0.72-0.77) on the UCSF dataset (n = 2247 studies; 30% reduced RVSF).
evidence.sample_unit: coronary angiography studies (development set; also 2247 UCSF external studies, 82 prospective STEMI cases, 200 human-evaluation cases)

evidence.title: AI-ECG Detection of Structural Heart Disease in the Community Setting: Transportability and Spectrum Effects in the PREVUE-VALVE Study
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
evidence.outcome: AI-ECG discrimination in community population versus hospital-based derivation cohort
evidence.effect: AUC 71% (95% CI 66%-76%) in PREVUE-VALVE vs 83% (95% CI 82%-83%) in hospital cohort; SHD prevalence 8% vs 43%; propensity matching attenuated but did not eliminate the difference.
evidence.quote: Consistent with these differences, model discrimination was lower in PREVUE-VALVE than in the hospital-based cohort (AUC: 71% [95% CI: 66%-76%] vs 83% [95% CI: 82%-83%]).
evidence.sample_unit: community-dwelling participants aged 65-85 with in-home ECG and echocardiography

evidence.title: Organ-Agents: Virtual Human Physiology Simulator via LLMs
evidence.outcome: Simulation accuracy under distribution shift on external ICU cohorts from two hospitals
evidence.effect: External validation on 22,689 ICU patients from two hospitals showed moderate degradation under distribution shifts, though simulation remained stable.
evidence.quote: External validation on 22,689 ICU patients from two hospitals showed moderate degradation under distribution shifts with stable simulation.

evidence.title: Securing Collaborative Medical AI by Using Differential Privacy: Domain Transfer for Classification of Chest Radiographs
evidence.outcome: AUC drop from single-institution to cross-institution performance across five chest radiograph datasets
evidence.effect: Cross-institutional AUC decreased by 0.07 (VinDr-CXR), 0.07 (ChestX-ray14), 0.07 (CheXpert), 0.18 (UKA-CXR), and 0.07 (PadChest) for DP-DT, with similar drops for non-DP models.
evidence.quote: Even with high privacy levels (ε ≈ 1), DP-DT showed no evidence of differences compared with non–DP-DT in terms of a decrease in AUC of cross-institutional performance as compared with single-institutional performance (VinDr-CXR: 0.07 vs 0.07, P = .96; ChestX-ray14: 0.07 vs 0.06, P = .12; CheXpert: 0.07 vs 0.07, P = .18; UKA-CXR: 0.18 vs 0.18, P = .90; and PadChest: 0.07 vs 0.07, P = .35).

evidence.title: Domain shifts decrease the accuracy of machine learning algorithms to detect myocardial ischemia in ECG recordings: A multi-database analysis
evidence.outcome: Effect of dataset shift between development and external datasets on model performance
evidence.effect: Variations in ECG patterns across datasets contributed to performance drops; sensitivity decreased substantially when tested on different datasets.
evidence.quote: Further analysis showed that variations in ECG patterns across datasets contributed to these differences in performance.

evidence.title: Calibration Drift Under Cross-Institutional Deployment: An External Validation Framework for ICU Mortality Prediction Across MIMIC-IV and eICU
evidence.outcome: Prevalence-driven label shift
evidence.effect: External validation showed systematic risk overestimation with intercept −0.678, attributed to prevalence-driven label shift.
evidence.quote: Internal calibration was near-ideal (slope 0.982; intercept 0.001), whereas external validation revealed systematic risk overestimation (intercept − 0.678) attributable to prevalence-driven label shift.

evidence.title: Cross-Cohort Generalizability of Plasma Biomarker Machine Learning Models Reveals Calibration-Driven Degradation in Clinical Utility
evidence.outcome: Biomarker distribution differences between development and external cohorts indicating dataset shift
evidence.effect: Biomarker distribution differences across ADNI and A4 were consistent with dataset shift, and cross-cohort transfer degraded predictive values despite preserved discrimination.
evidence.quote: Biomarker distribution differences across cohorts were consistent with dataset shift.

evidence.title: Agentic Trial Emulation to Learn Health System-specific Drug Effects At Scale
evidence.outcome: Systematic shift between trial evidence and local EHR-derived effect estimates
evidence.effect: Posterior institution-specific shift consistently positive across folds (median 0.364–0.580), indicating systematic attenuation of DOAC benefit in the local EHR beyond literature-expected disagreement.
evidence.quote: The posterior institution-specific shift was consistently positive across folds (median 0.364–0.580), indicating systematic attenuation of DOAC benefit in the local EHR beyond literature-expected disagreement; residual heterogeneity was moderate (median 0.199–0.264).
evidence.sample_unit: trials emulated (three independent agent runs each)

evidence.title: Performance of a Chinese Cognitive Decline Risk Model in a Japanese Cohort: A Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Discrimination and calibration of Chinese-derived model in Japanese external cohort
evidence.effect: External AUC 0.68 (vs 0.62 in development set), but calibration slope 1.54, indicating systematic underestimation of absolute risk in the low-prevalence Japanese population.
evidence.quote: However, a notable calibration shift was observed (Slope = 1.54), indicating a systematic underestimation of absolute risk in the low-prevalence Japanese population.
evidence.sample_unit: cognitively normal older adults in derivation cohort (plus 1,333 temporal and 2,798 external validation)

evidence.title: From National Data to Local Evaluation: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Perioperative Risk Prediction
evidence.outcome: Model ranking consistency between national test data and a single-institution deployment check
evidence.effect: Rankings changed under AUPRC and did not hold in a 3,490-case single-institution deployment check.
evidence.quote: Rankings changed under AUPRC and did not hold in a 3,490-case single-institution deployment check, not independent of the PUF.
evidence.sample_unit: surgical cases (temporal test set, 2024 ACS NSQIP)

evidence.title: External validation reveals poor calibration despite preserved discrimination for a vasopressin treatment-signal prediction model across ICU databases
evidence.outcome: Discrimination and calibration of frozen model on external database vs internal test
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.768 internally and 0.746 externally; external calibration-in-the-large −0.712 (overprediction) with slope 0.446.
evidence.quote: The model retained cross-database discrimination but not calibrated absolute risk.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU stays (3,692 training, 1,582 MIMIC-IV internal test, 1,801 eICU-CRD external)

evidence.title: Comparing Deep Learning Models for Lung Nodule Detection on Photon-Counting CT Images in a Non-Screening Setting
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and false positives of models developed for conventional CT when applied to PCCT
evidence.effect: Sensitivity moderate, 0.71 (95% CI 0.64-0.77) to 0.83 (0.77-0.88); TotalSegmentator and RadYOLO had 0.85 false positives per scan (95% CI 0.70-1.02).
evidence.quote: The models showed moderate sensitivity (between 0.71, 95%-CI [0.64, 0.77], and 0.83, 95%-CI [0.77, 0.88]), and TotalSegmentator and RadYOLO produced few false positives per scan (both 0.85, 95%-CI [0.70, 1.02]).

evidence.title: Accuracy and generalizability of machine learning models for adolescent suicide prediction with longitudinal clinical records
evidence.outcome: Performance drop when transporting suicide prediction models to new datasets
evidence.effect: Transfer performance declined versus local: average AUC reduced by up to 7.7%, sensitivity by up to 16% and PPV by up to 2% at 90% specificity; sensitivity by up to 20% and PPV by up to 5% at 95% specificity.
evidence.quote: Significant and comparable decreases in the transfer performance compared to the local performance of all three ML models were observed, with the decline in performance reducing average AUC by up to 7.7%, reducing average sensitivity by up to 16%, and PPV by up to 2% at the 90% specificity level, and reducing sensitivity by up to 20% and PPV by up to 5% at the 95% specificity level.

evidence.title: Evaluation of a Machine Learning-guided Strategy for Elevated Lipoprotein(a) Screening in Health Systems
evidence.outcome: Difference between Lp(a)-tested population and other cohorts in ARISE features
evidence.effect: The Lp(a) tested population significantly differed from other study cohorts (UK Biobank, ARIC, CARDIA, MESA) in terms of ARISE features.
evidence.quote: The Lp(a) tested population significantly differed from other study cohorts in terms of ARISE features.
evidence.sample_unit: randomly sampled YNHHS patients (plus 7,981 YNHHS and 10,635 VUMC Lp(a)-tested patients)

evidence.title: Generalizability of Clinical Prediction Models in Mental Health - Real-World Validation of Machine Learning Models for Depressive Symptom Prediction
evidence.outcome: Generalization of depressive symptom prediction model across diverse inpatient and outpatient samples
evidence.effect: Sparse model trained on clinical information generalized strongly across diverse real-world samples despite systematic differences between samples; no numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Despite systematic differences between samples, a sparse machine learning model trained on clinical information exhibited strong generalization across diverse real-world samples.

evidence.title: Hazard-aware adaptations bridge the generalization gap in large language models: a nationwide study
evidence.outcome: Error hazard distributions between development-like (MIMIC) and VA institutional datasets
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy was similar (macro-F1 0.86 VA, 0.85 MIMIC), but hazard distributions varied significantly; templated information more prevalent in VA notes (p adj=0.004).
evidence.quote: While overall accuracy with the adapted prompt was similar between institutions (macro-F1=0.86 in VA, 0.85 in MIMIC), hazard distributions varied significantly.
evidence.sample_unit: notes and LLM outputs analyzed for error codification

evidence.title: Multisite evaluation of prediction models for emergency department crowding before and during the COVID-19 pandemic
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Model AUC when transferred between hospitals with different populations and settings
evidence.effect: Model trained at location 2 and tested at location 1 had AUC 0.69 pre-COVID (drop of 0.09) and 0.51 during COVID-era (drop of 0.27) versus location 1-trained model.
evidence.quote: For example, a model trained at location 2 and tested at location 1 had an AUC of 0.69 during pre-COVID (a drop of 0.09 from the location 1 trained model) and an AUC 0.51 during the COVID-era (a drop of 0.27 from the location 1 trained model).
evidence.sample_unit: ED encounters (62,585 + 34,244 at location 1; 24,992 + 17,359 at location 2)

evidence.title: External validation and update of the J-ACCESS model in an Italian cohort of patients undergoing stress myocardial perfusion imaging
evidence.venue: Journal of nuclear cardiology : official publication of the American Society of Nuclear Cardiology
evidence.outcome: Underestimation of risk due to cohort differences in event rate between development and local cohorts
evidence.effect: MACE rate 8.2% locally vs 4.3% in J-ACCESS (P<.001); model underestimated observed risk; Hosmer-Lemeshow 214.9, P<.001.
evidence.quote: The percentage of our patients with MACE was 8.2%, significantly higher compared to the 4.3% found in the J-ACCESS study ( P < .001).

evidence.title: Multicentre external validation of a commercial artificial intelligence software to analyse chest radiographs in health screening environments with low disease prevalence
evidence.outcome: Performance drop when applying AI in a setting differing from its training setting
evidence.effect: AI performance in low-prevalence health screening was poorer than expected, suggesting experimental/regulatory performance may not translate to real-world practice.
evidence.quote: The technical prowess of AI demonstrated in experimental settings and approved by regulatory bodies may not directly translate to real-world practice, especially where the demand for AI assistance is highest.

evidence.title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
evidence.venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
evidence.outcome: Differences between development and local cohorts and resulting miscalibration
evidence.effect: Croce cohort had more penetrating trauma (23% vs 3%), younger patients (median 35 vs 51), more laparotomy (14% vs 3%); pneumonia incidence 5.6% vs 10.6%; calibration slope 0.63.
evidence.quote: However, in Croce’s cohort, the incidence of penetrating trauma was higher (23% vs. 3%), patients were younger (median 35 vs. 51 years), and relatively more patients underwent an emergent laparotomy (14% vs. 3%) compared to the Dutch cohort [ 6 ].

evidence.title: Is the generalizability of a developed artificial intelligence algorithm for COVID-19 on chest CT sufficient for clinical use? Results from the International Consortium for COVID-19 Imaging AI (ICOVAI)
evidence.outcome: Performance drop when applied to data from other institutions than development
evidence.effect: Significant reduction in lung opacity segmentation (DSC 0.76 to 0.59) and CO-RADS agreement (kappa 0.78 to 0.62) on external multicenter data.
evidence.quote: Our work shows that published results of COVID-19 segmentation on internal test sets may not generalize well to patient data from other institutions.

evidence.title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
evidence.outcome: Differences between development and local populations and resulting miscalibration
evidence.effect: Local patients younger (53 vs 65 years), more critical preoperative state (9.8% vs 4.1%), more elective surgery (94% vs 77%); scores underestimated mortality in all risk groups
evidence.quote: The patients were younger (53 vs. 65 years), had lower creatinine clearance (74.97 mL/min vs. 83.6 mL/min), were more often in critical preoperative state (9.8% vs. 4.1%), and a higher proportion had elective surgery (94% vs. 77%) than in the EuroSCORE II population.

evidence.title: Computed tomography and radiation dose images-based deep-learning model for predicting radiation pneumonitis in lung cancer patients after radiation therapy
evidence.venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
evidence.outcome: Performance on cohorts with different settings
evidence.effect: Baseline AUC dropped from 0.83 in test-set-1 to 0.55 and 0.63 in RTOG-0617 cohorts.
evidence.quote: The discriminative ability of a baseline trained model had an AUC of 0.83 for test-set-1, 0.55 for test-set-2, and 0.63 for test-set-3.

evidence.title: Decision-making support systems on extended hospital length of stay: Validation and recalibration of a model for patients with AMI
evidence.outcome: Generalizability of model developed at small hospital to larger hospital population
evidence.effect: Model developed on a ~400-bed hospital did not generalize to a ~1,000-bed hospital in a different period; AUC dropped 0.828 to 0.702 and predictor ORs and CIs differed.
evidence.quote: Therefore, it highlights the need to recalibrate the models to new populations, as the models cannot be generalized to different populations without losing their predictive capacity.

evidence.title: Utility of an Artificial Intelligence Enabled Electrocardiogram for Risk Assessment in Liver Transplant Candidates
evidence.outcome: AI-ECG performance in liver transplant evaluation patients versus general population, and by QTc
evidence.effect: Performance in LT evaluation patients was similar to the general population but lower with prolonged QTc; AUROC 0.69 for post-transplant AF and 0.69 for later low LVEF.
evidence.quote: The performance of AI-ECG in patients undergoing LT evaluation is similar to that in a general population but was lower in the presence of prolonged QTc.

evidence.title: Technical Adequacy of Fully Automated Artificial Intelligence Body Composition Tools: Assessment in a Heterogeneous Sample of External CT Examinations
evidence.outcome: Tool failure rate on external CT data differing from local development data
evidence.effect: At least one tool failed in 268 (2.3%) of examinations; individual adequacy 97.8% bone, 99.1% muscle, 98.9% fat.
evidence.quote: At least one tool failed in 268 (2.3%) of the examinations.

evidence.title: Deep Neural Network Augments Performance of Junior Residents in Diagnosing COVID-19 Pneumonia on Chest Radiographs
evidence.outcome: Model performance drop from internal to external test set (domain shift)
evidence.effect: AUC 0.9518 on internal test set versus 0.8594 on external test set; authors suggest domain shift between datasets.
evidence.quote: This suggests a domain shift between the patient dataset and the external dataset, highlighting the need for future research on test-time training domain adaptation to address this issue.
evidence.sample_unit: external test chest radiographs read by 3 junior residents with and without AI

evidence.title: Development, multi-institutional external validation, and algorithmic audit of an artificial intelligence-based Side-specific Extra-Prostatic Extension Risk Assessment tool (SEPERA) for patients undergoing radical prostatectomy: a retrospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: Generalisation from community-hospital training data to external academic centres in three sites
evidence.effect: Trained on 1022 cases from a community hospital network and externally validated on 3914 cases at three academic centres, SEPERA was well calibrated with pooled AUROC 0.77 across validation cohorts.
evidence.quote: SEPERA was well calibrated and had the best performance across all validation cohorts (pooled AUROC of 0·77 [95% CI 0·75-0·78] and pooled AUPRC of 0·61 [0·58-0·63]).

evidence.title: Evaluating the performance of artificial intelligence software for lung nodule detection on chest radiographs in a retrospective real-world UK population
evidence.outcome: Generalisability of training/testing data to local population; false positive failure analysis
evidence.effect: Normal or variant anatomy misidentified as abnormality in 69.9% of 943 false positives; lack of generalisability in training and testing datasets suggested as factor.
evidence.quote: Failure analysis suggested a lack of generalisability in the training and testing datasets as a potential factor.

evidence.title: External evaluation of the Dynamic Criticality Index: A machine learning model to predict future need for ICU care in hospitalized pediatric patients
evidence.outcome: Differences in model covariate importance and practice patterns between development and local setting

evidence.title: Concordance and generalization of an AI algorithm with real-world clinical data in the pre-omicron and omicron era

evidence.title: Application of MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections

evidence.title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults

evidence.title: Recalibration of a Non-Laboratory-Based Risk Model to Estimate Pre-Diabetes/Diabetes Mellitus Risk in Primary Care in Hong Kong

evidence.title: Metabolic syndrome risk prediction in an Australian sample with first-episode psychosis using the psychosis metabolic risk calculator: A validation study

evidence.title: Addressing the implementation challenge of risk prediction model due to missing risk factors: The submodel approximation approach

evidence.title: From theoretical models to practical deployment: A perspective and case study of opportunities and challenges in AI-driven cardiac auscultation research for low-income settings
evidence.outcome: Generalisation of heart murmur detection models to out-of-distribution data

evidence.title: Validation of 30-Day Pediatric Hospital Readmission Risk Prediction Models

evidence.title: External Validation of a Winning Artificial Intelligence Algorithm from the RSNA 2022 Cervical Spine Fracture Detection Challenge

evidence.quote: The external validation data set comprised older patients in comparison to the competition set (53.5 ± 21.8 years versus 58 ± 22.0, respectively; P < .05).

evidence.title: External validation of an algorithm to detect vertebral level mislabeling and autocontouring errors

commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources endorse comparing development and local populations, and four offline or benchmark studies show that such comparisons can surface differences and, in one case, flag a shifted cohort with lower accuracy. No study tested whether the comparison changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes, and one found that performance held despite large population differences.

perspectives.view: Four studies examined the practice, all at level 4 or 5 and none in live deployment. Each described differences between development and local data, and one found that a cohort applicability score of 48% matched the lowest accuracy of 53%. No study measured effects on decisions or outcomes, so certainty is very low.

In one hazard study, local prevalence was 4.1% against 45.0-62.2% in the manufacturer's populations, and local PPV was 33% against 95-98% reported. A comparison may reveal such gaps before go-live. One test found large population differences with stable performance, which suggests the comparison flags risk but does not replace local performance testing.

The ward study compared 52 features and found that missingness differed by more than 5% in 9 of them, with deterioration rates of 4.5% versus 2.5%. Hazard studies tie performance drops to documentation and service setting, such as a coding F-score falling from 0.754 to 0.620 and theme accuracy of 57% in community and mental health services.

The Finnish psychosis study found that 100% versus 55.3% of patients were White European or not reported across samples, and the ward study found 20% versus 49% non-White patients. Neither reported insurance, language, or literacy. A Kenyan hazard study found a younger population with more diabetes and hypertension than the UK Biobank development cohort.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors who use data from outside the United States to explain how disease presentation, prevalence, and demographics compare with American patients and medical practice. This assigns part of the comparison to manufacturers. Local teams still depend on vendors disclosing development populations, and none of the studies assessed how often that disclosure occurs.

commentary.research_gap: No study measured whether a structured comparison of development and local populations before go-live changed adoption decisions, prompted recalibration, or reduced harm in live use. No study reported what the comparison costs in staff time or data access. Studies that pair the comparison with local performance testing could show which differences, such as missingness, prevalence, or scanner type, predict degradation and which do not.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The ward study reported race only, with 49% non-White patients at the external site. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether the comparison detects the shifts most likely to affect their patients, such as differences in documentation, language, or access to follow-up care.
